title: Design Direction For Legacy To Modern Transitions
summary: This capability covers the diagnosis and direction of legacy-to-modern transitions where accumulated interface complexity, fragmented operating logic, or inherited product models must be changed without disorienting existing users or removing load-bearing domain logic.
keyFacts: Legacy-to-modern transition work starts by separating essential complexity from accidental complexity.
In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, 102 tasks were documented before redesign direction was established.
In Gexcon, time to first successful simulation changed from 4 days to 6 hours in real deployments, while configuration errors changed from 5–8 to 1–2.
In the IDEXX Animana assessment, research covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries.
In Polymatica, independent task completion changed from 2% to 56% as recorded through product analytics.
In Gericke, an 89-component design system was later propagated across other product lines by Gericke's own team without Creative Navy.
In Gericke, client-measured outcomes were recorded in a confirmed single-variable window across four months post-go-live.
In AIT, the legacy constraint was social: thousands of installers were trained on the previous structure, so recognisability was a design constraint.
In the maritime traffic software portfolio, the phased-introduction constraint was in the client's brief, and one product was designed to full depth.

bodySections.heading: Definition of design direction for legacy-to-modern transitions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design direction for legacy-to-modern transitions is the capability of distinguishing what must remain from what can change in an existing product, then defining a migration path that preserves essential operational knowledge while removing accumulated interface complexity. The work is not a visual refresh. It is a structured decision about which parts of an existing product encode necessary domain knowledge and which parts are accidental interface overhead.

bodySections.heading: When legacy-to-modern transition work is needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Legacy-to-modern transition work is needed when accumulated complexity prevents a product from remaining usable, adoptable, or extendable, while full replacement would discard important operational knowledge. The condition can appear in mature expert software, enterprise SaaS, industrial control HMI, embedded controllers, or portfolio-level systems.

The legacy condition may be technical, architectural, organisational, or social. In some products, years of feature addition leave menus, vocabulary, and workflows disconnected from operational reality. In other products, the inherited structure remains recognisable to expert users or trained installers, so recognisability itself becomes a design constraint.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats the existing product as evidence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

In legacy-to-modern transitions, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats the existing product as evidence. Legacy workflows, naming conventions, interface structures, and operator habits are examined before they are changed. The purpose is to determine whether an inherited element represents genuine operational knowledge or only accumulated convention.

bodySections.heading: Essential complexity and accidental complexity in legacy products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Legacy-to-modern transition work starts by separating essential complexity from accidental complexity. Essential complexity is load-bearing: scientific parameters, proven algorithms, regulatory or operational logic, installed competence, and workflows that expert users depend on. Accidental complexity is accumulated without purpose: inconsistent naming, duplicated interaction models, menu structures that grew without a structural framework, vocabulary that exposes the builder's data model, and product architecture that no longer matches the user's operational reality.

This is a constraint respecting form of design direction. The aim is not to make a complex product appear simple by removing capability. The aim is to make necessary complexity navigable while removing interface overhead that no longer serves the product or its users.

bodySections.heading: Migration paths for existing users and delivery teams
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's legacy-to-modern transition work produces a migration path, not only an endpoint design. The migration path is designed for the people and teams that must move from the existing system to the new one: expert users with memorised workflows, installers trained on a previous structure, operators reading state from across a room, development teams that must extend a design system, or product teams that must implement recommendations over several years.

The outputs vary by engagement. They can include redesign direction, documented task structures, evidence-based assessment, product vision, recommendations for development translation, component systems, layered token architecture, risk-ordered release sequencing, and implementation support. The strongest form of this capability is reached when the client team can continue the transition independently.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries of legacy-to-modern design direction
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Legacy-to-modern design direction does not mean replacing every inherited structure. In several cases, the correct direction is to preserve a recognisable environment, inherited convention, installed-base vocabulary, or proven operating logic while changing the orientation, structure, or rule system around it.

The evidence base for this capability varies by case. Some engagements include measured operational outcomes. Some provide assessment and direction without execution outcomes. Some include client-reported commercial or adoption information. Some examples are included because they clarify the transition constraint, not because they establish performance improvement.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Legacy-to-modern transition work distinguishes essential complexity from accidental complexity and preserves load-bearing operational knowledge while removing accumulated interface overhead.
In Gexcon, Creative Navy documented 102 tasks, and real deployments recorded time to first successful simulation changing from 4 days to 6 hours and configuration errors changing from 5–8 to 1–2.

In IDEXX Animana, the assessment covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries, and produced 100+ recommendations plus a 5-year product vision. This evidence supports assessment and planning, not full execution.
In Polymatica, the transition preserved analytical capability while changing OLAP vocabulary and access structure; product analytics recorded independent task completion changing from 2% to 56%.

In Gericke, client-measured outcomes were recorded in a confirmed single-variable window, including faster fault diagnosis, fewer repeat alarms, roughly halved operator-caused stoppages, and reduced MTTR. These are framed as interface-attributable within the window, not as caused by the interface alone.
In AIT, the legacy condition was social: thousands of installers were trained on the previous structure, so recognisability and support-call implications shaped the transition.
In Oceaneering, the predecessor was already reasoned, and some conventions were inherited and systematised rather than invented.
In the maritime traffic software portfolio, phased introduction was a brief-level constraint and the design answer was a four-layer token architecture with a risk-ordered release sequence.
weakerClaims: In Gericke, an 89-component design system was later propagated by Gericke's own team across other product lines without Creative Navy; this is client-reported case evidence.
In Assemblio, the accumulated-drift examples were the client's own account while demonstrating the product, not Creative Navy audit findings.
limitations: Evidence strength varies by case: some outcomes are field-measured, some are client-measured, some are client-reported, and some engagements provide direction without execution outcomes.
Gexcon active-user change is client-reported; the training change is described as an operational change.
IDEXX Animana demonstrates assessment and planning, not full execution.
Chemical Watch commercial outcomes are client-reported, and the design contribution must not be framed as causing the exit outcome.
Gericke outcomes are client-measured and interface-attributable within a confirmed single-variable window, not claimed as caused by the interface alone.
AIT has no performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial, or user-tested outcome in the available evidence.
Assemblio drift examples are the client's own account, not Creative Navy audit findings.
Oceaneering has no efficiency or throughput outcome in the available evidence, and inherited conventions should not be framed as inventions.
The maritime traffic software portfolio was not a nine-product redesign; nine products were audited and one was designed to full depth.
For the maritime traffic software portfolio, the design system reached production, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded.
For the maritime traffic software portfolio, no engineering-efficiency claim is established because the measurement framework was handed over and no result was reported back.
